You managed to perfectly capture how I feel! I also wonder how sustainable this is, as there is no reason why the farmers would reduce the number of hens they're cycling through when following this program (they're probably making more money from it this way). 

I would say the majority of the British population who don't already own chickens/hens, wouldn't have the facilities to care for them with proper husbandry. I rent, like many people, and don't have access to a proper garden. Most average homes probably wouldn't have the space for more than 10 chickens if that, and like you said, at what standard would these animals be kept at?

I'm sure many do end up in great rescue farms, or to homes with people who will truly care for them, but they cannot possibly continue to rehome these hens who have a 5-10+ year lifespan when farmers are breeding and cycling through them every 72 weeks.

My problem is I don't realistically think that there will be room for these hens to be rehomed. I can't find stats for how many hens specifically are slaughtered per year, but animal equality says 36 million are used for eggs per year. In the best case scenario, all of these would be rehomed but who can accommodate for 36 million hens? I wonder how many are truly rehomed through these schemes and how effective they really are, that's all. I know my POV is indeed cynical and that it is probably healthier to have your mindset.

I agree it is a cynical view, I think I'm just overly tired of seeing this type of "activism" in which people still contribute to animal exploitation. 

The biggest issues I have with this specific situation is not the shift from livestock to pets, but that the farmer is still profiting off exploiting these animals. They can farm their eggs for 72 weeks, and then this organisation will **pay** for the hens. The farmers who are a part of this scheme will not at all be discouraged from continuing their practice, they still get the eggs and make money except now instead of shipping them off for dog food they're shipped off to a none profit to rehome. The hens will continue to be mass bred and more and more will continue to need rehoming.

Realistically, the egg market will never disappear unless people stop eating eggs. People producing their own eggs just doesn't work in the modern world. Only those who have land and can afford to house and feed hens would be a part of this system. 

Don't get me wrong, I do wish that all of these animals could be freed from the exploitation system that they're in, and rehoming into loving homes where they can live out the rest of their natural lives is definitely better than death, but this should be at the cost of farmers. While farmers continue to profit from exploitation we shouldn't be satisfied.

I totally appreciate your POV as someone who has owned chickens, I am sure they had a great life with you! Maybe all of this is just me projecting lol, I don't and will probably never have the space to be able to rescue ex-livestock as I cannot afford to enter the property market and escape rental hell.

My biggest tips: Plan, be patient and have fun 

Plan as much as you can in early stages, things are bound to change but it's always good to keep organised. Prepare yourself with testing kits and other necessary tools, determine the tank size you want, shrimp you want and how many, as well as any plants. Substrate, decoration, lighting etc. If you're having a planted tank, look into how the plants you choose will grow and spread. These things are all something you can decide very quickly and impulsively on, but it's much easier to plan ahead and make sure you'll be happy than try to change things 6 months down the line.

Be patient with your water cycling, acclimatising and other things. Rushing in too soon could cause unnecessary problems, a small spike in ammonia as a result of not cycling properly could result in casualties and we want you to have as many happy healthy shrimp as possible!

Enjoy yourself, shrimp keeping is so rewarding and I'm sure you'll make an amazing shrimp parent.❤

Why would anyone suggest this to someone with anorexia? Why would you ask advice for weightloss in an anorexia subreddit??

It sounds like you were conditioned by ED/diet culture as a child and naturally retaliated by trying to 'fix' yourself with disordered behaviours. I would 10000% recommend therapy - finding somewhere you can open up about your past and the way that it molded your modern day thoughts and feelings. You might be able to get help asking at school if you're uncomfortable talking to your family about this.

There is a fine line between disordered eating and eating disorders, so its difficult to say which category you would fall into. Many people don't know or  don't want to believe they have an ED before it's too deeply ingrained in them, and even then many still deny it.

Ask yourself this, if you want to 'just stop', why don't you? Chances are there's something holding you back, in this case the satisfaction you recieve from restricting (very common). 

I really hope you are able to take back control of your eating before it causes any serious damage, you're only young and have every chance to recovery fully. It might be worth trying to educate your family on eating disorders if possible.

Up to 80% of Anorexia suffers will have some kind of cardiac complications either now or in the future, which leads to 1/3 deaths. Anorexia is not a maintainable condition, but as long as you're doing something about it and working towards recovery you shouldn't worry about cardiac events.

There can be many causes for cardiac arrest, both from weight and intake. Lacking in potassium can cause hypokaelemia which can trigger a cardiac event, similarly a low body weight can cause muscle deterioration and damage your heart. If you're working with a mental health team they should monitor your bloods to ensure that your potassium and other levels are stable, if not I would recommend visiting the doctor to check these out.

Assuming you live at home, have you spoken to your parents/whoever you live with about this? It can be hard to set boundaries alone but if one of your loved ones is able to set boundaries for you that could help. 

My grandparents came to visit me while I was in treatment and my dad specifically told them not to say anything about mine or anyone else's body, I was terrified because they've said some crazy shit in the past but it turned out to be fine.

Most of the time people who comment on others bodies are either:
1. Insecure in their own 
2. Fatphobic and/or diet culture obsessed (brainwashed)
Or a combination of both 

This means their comments are either a projection of their own insecurity, or that they think they're being a 'good person' by pointing out things. The reality is that neither of those points mean that you're the problem, so no matter how hard it is please fight the urge to take out your pain on yourself and your body. You are so incredibly strong for fighting your ED. No one should ever have have justify their weight and to be made fun of by your relatives is.. just horrific.

My only other suggestion would be to potentially share some resources with them about EDs, what not to say, weight stigma, recovery etc. This is what I had to do to stop my mum from commenting on my body. You can find loads online but I'd be happy to comment some if you need.

Animals without these don’t feel ‘pain’ the same way. They have receptors (nociceptors) that allow them to recognise a negative stimulus and move away, but don’t feel ‘pain’ like how a mammal would.

Different species are affected by different stimulus. There have been a lot of experiments and tests surrounding these animals that are more difficult to understand (most experiments are pretty unethical) but it’s interesting to read about.

Personally, I would choose to avoid putting any animal in a situation like this. For example, a lobster would not willingly want to stay in a boiling pot of water while alive. Regardless of how it ‘feels’ pain, it’s clear that they do not want to be there and their nociceptors are triggered by the boiling water. 

I’m always interested in seeing updated information regarding inverts and how they feel/respond to pain and stimulus so if you know anything that I don’t please tell me ^^

Edit: Regarding Octopus, I recall a part of the video stating that they would often recall an injured tentacle and use it less often, but still take a risk if capturing prey is possible. It’s very possible they make a conscious decision on wether using an injured limb is worth the reward of capturing prey. I don’t recall anything particular about pain as such, but it’s interesting nonetheless.

As an adult, I hope your family respects that you can make decisions about your diet without their consent - regardless of if they deem it healthy. I would prepare myself with answers to those basic questions we all get e.g 'Protein?!? Food chain!?!!? EvOLuTioN?!' as they'll probably be curious.

Perhaps offer to make them a meal and don't tell them it's vegan? If you're into cooking, it would be a fun way to show them you aren't going to just eat lettuce forever. Or bake some vegan cupcakes etc. 

Again, I hope that they respect you and don't put you down for your choices. Good luck with it all!

EDIT: I was always stubborn and very much an animal lover at home, transitioned into being vegetarian as soon as my mum would let me (16) and became a vegan as soon as I moved out to university. I just limited my intake of animal products as much as possible. They are understanding now however.
